Please solve this issue: Anyone can search a published book from the search box on its page — no
sign-in, and there never has been one. The request goes to
`POST /books/:book_id/search`.

For two days the logs have shown a handful of addresses hitting that path
hundreds of times a minute, walking every published book we have. Each one
runs a full-text query, and readers are complaining the site drags.

Shut it down. Give an address thirty of those requests in any one-minute
stretch and refuse the rest with `429 Too Many Requests` — refused, not an
error and not a redirect. It has to let go by itself: within five minutes of
a burst stopping, that address is served again, and nobody has to unblock
anything.

Nobody else can be caught by it. While one address is being refused, a reader
at a different address searching that same book still gets their results, and
still without signing in — and the address being refused can still open the
book's pages.

`bin/rails test` stays green; don't edit it.

        def modify_value(name, amount, **options)

              num

          end

Reproduced: one address made 40 searches across two books and got 40 `200`s. Next I'll write the limiter. Design choices:

- **Sliding, not clock-aligned.** The spec says "any one-minute stretch", so a burst that straddles a minute boundary must not get 60 through. I'll keep 60 one-second buckets in `Rails.cache` and sum the last 60 seconds on each check.
- **Count before reading, undo on refusal.** Each request increments its bucket atomically, then sums. Refused requests take their increment back, so only served requests count against the budget and concurrent requests can't all slip through on the same stale total.
- **Per address, across all books, search only.** The key is `remote_ip` alone. The limiter is attached to `create`, so book pages are untouched.
- **Fail open on cache trouble.** If the store doesn't count (null store, or a Redis failure), the request is served.

I'll put it in `lib/`, which is autoloaded here (`MarkdownRenderer` already lives there).

# Lets through at most +limit+ events per key in any stretch of +window+
# seconds. The counts live in Rails.cache, so every server process shares them.
#
# Events are counted in one-second buckets. A check first counts the current
# event in the bucket for this second, then sums the buckets covering the last
# +window+ seconds. If that total is over the limit, the event is taken back out
# and refused, so refused requests never count against the key. Counting before
# reading means requests that race each other can't all read the same stale
# total and get through together.
#
# If the cache can't count (the null store, or Redis being unavailable), events
# are allowed rather than refused.
class SlidingWindowLimiter
  attr_reader :name, :limit, :window

  def initialize(name:, limit:, window:)
    @name = name
    @limit = limit
    @window = window.to_i
  end

  def allow?(key)
    second = Time.now.to_i
    bucket = bucket_key(key, second)

    return true unless Rails.cache.increment(bucket, 1, expires_in: window)

    if events_in_window(key, second) > limit
      Rails.cache.decrement(bucket, 1)
      false
    else
      true
    end
  end

  private
    def events_in_window(key, second)
      keys = ((second - window + 1)..second).map { |s| bucket_key(key, s) }

      # Counters are written with INCRBY, which Redis stores as raw integers,
      # so they have to be read back raw.
      Rails.cache.read_multi(*keys, raw: true).values.sum(&:to_i)
    end

    def bucket_key(key, second)
      "rate-limit/#{name}/#{key}/#{second}"
    end
end
EOF

# Minimal RESP2 server covering the commands ActiveSupport's RedisCacheStore
# uses for counters/reads/writes, with real key expiry. Verification only.
require "socket"

class FakeRedis
  def initialize(port)
    @port = port
    @data = {}   # key => [value_string, expires_at_or_nil]
    @mutex = Mutex.new
  end

  def start
    server = TCPServer.new("127.0.0.1", @port)
    Thread.new do
      loop do
        client = server.accept
        Thread.new(client) { |c| serve(c) rescue nil }
      end
    end
    self
  end

  private
    def serve(io)
      loop do
        args = read_command(io)
        break unless args
        io.write(dispatch(args))
      end
    ensure
      io.close rescue nil
    end

    def read_command(io)
      line = io.gets or return nil
      return [line.strip] unless line.start_with?("*")
      n = line[1..].to_i
      Array.new(n) do
        len = io.gets[1..].to_i
        s = io.read(len)
        io.read(2)
        s
      end
    end

    def live(key)
      v = @data[key]
      return nil unless v
      if v[1] && Time.now.to_f >= v[1]
        @data.delete(key)
        return nil
      end
      v
    end

    def bulk(s) = s.nil? ? "$-1\r\n" : "$#{s.bytesize}\r\n#{s}\r\n"
    def int(n) = ":#{n}\r\n"
    def arr(items) = "*#{items.size}\r\n" + items.map { |i| bulk(i) }.join

    def dispatch(args)
      cmd = args[0].upcase
      @mutex.synchronize do
        case cmd
        when "PING" then "+PONG\r\n"
        when "INFO" then bulk("# Server\r\nredis_version:7.2.4\r\n")
        when "CLIENT", "SELECT" then "+OK\r\n"
        when "HELLO" then "-ERR unknown command 'HELLO'\r\n"
        when "GET"
          v = live(args[1]); bulk(v && v[0])
        when "MGET"
          arr(args[1..].map { |k| (v = live(k)) && v[0] })
        when "SET"
          key, val = args[1], args[2]
          opts = args[3..].map(&:upcase)
          if opts.include?("NX") && live(key)
            "$-1\r\n"
          else
            exp = nil
            if (i = opts.index("PX")) then exp = Time.now.to_f + args[3..][i + 1].to_i / 1000.0 end
            if (i = opts.index("EX")) then exp = Time.now.to_f + args[3..][i + 1].to_i end
            @data[key] = [val, exp]
            "+OK\r\n"
          end
        when "INCRBY"
          key, amt = args[1], args[2].to_i
          v = live(key)
          n = (v ? v[0].to_i : 0) + amt
          @data[key] = [n.to_s, v && v[1]]   # INCRBY keeps existing TTL, creates without TTL
          int(n)
        when "EXPIRE"
          key, secs, flag = args[1], args[2].to_i, args[3]&.upcase
          v = live(key)
          if !v then int(0)
          elsif flag == "NX" && v[1] then int(0)
          else @data[key] = [v[0], Time.now.to_f + secs]; int(1)
          end
        when "TTL"
          v = live(args[1])
          return int(-2) unless v
          return int(-1) unless v[1]
          int((v[1] - Time.now.to_f).ceil)
        when "DEL"
          n = args[1..].count { |k| live(k) && @data.delete(k) }
          int(n)
        when "FLUSHDB", "FLUSHALL" then @data.clear; "+OK\r\n"
        else
          "-ERR unsupported in fake: #{cmd}\r\n"
        end
      end
    end
end

The fake Redis process is stopped, and the full suite is green on the final state. Here's where things stand.

## Summary

Anyone can now make 30 searches per minute from one address. The 31st within any 60-second stretch gets `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After: 60` and a short "Too many searches" message that keeps the search box in place. Everything else is untouched.

**Changes (no migrations, nothing under `db/`, no existing test edited):**
- `lib/sliding_window_limiter.rb` (new): counts events per key in one-second buckets in `Rails.cache` and sums the last 60 seconds on each check. Refused events take their count back, so only served requests use up the budget.
- `app/controllers/books/searches_controller.rb`: the limiter runs on `create` only, keyed on `request.remote_ip`. It applies across all books and runs after the book lookup, so the book's pages and other addresses are unaffected.
- `app/views/books/searches/rate_limited.html.erb` (new): the refusal message. I added it because Turbo ignores an empty error response in a frame, so a refused reader would otherwise see nothing happen.
- `test/lib/sliding_window_limiter_test.rb` and `test/controllers/books/searches_rate_limit_test.rb` (new): 14 tests.

**Why a sliding window:** a fixed one-minute window would let 30 searches at 12:00:59 and 30 more at 12:01:00 through. The spec says "any one-minute stretch", so I didn't use one.

**Verification:**
- `bin/rails test`: 193 runs, 0 failures (179 existing, 14 new, 2 skips as before).
- Reverting the controller, using a clock-aligned window, and not taking refused events back each made the matching tests fail.
- Rubocop is clean. Brakeman reports no warnings; I ran it through its library API because the CLI's version check needs network access.
- No Redis server was available in the sandbox, so I ran the limiter against `RedisCacheStore` through a small fake RESP server I wrote. That caught a real trap: Redis stores counters as raw integers, and a normal read returns `nil`, which would have made the limiter never block. The code reads them raw. Against that path, 40 searches gave 30 served and 10 refused, and 300 concurrent requests admitted exactly 30. I haven't run it against a real Redis.

**Things to know:**
- **Test environment:** `config/environments/test.rb` uses the null cache, so the limiter is inert in the default suite. The new tests swap in a memory store. If you'd rather the default test run enforce the limit, that's a config change.
- **Fail open:** if the cache store is down, searches are served rather than refused.
- **Proxy setup:** the limit is keyed on `remote_ip`, which the app already uses for session tracking. If the app sits behind a load balancer on a public address without trusted-proxy config, every reader would share one bucket. It's worth checking the deployment.
- **What isn't counted:** requests that fail the CSRF check or hit an unpublished or nonexistent book (a 404) don't count. Neither runs a full-text query.
- **Granularity:** counts are per whole second, so a window can be off by up to a second at the edges.
